issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' is hard to reconcile with simultaneously becoming so overwhelmed on recall that she has to stop and experiencing intense rage when remembering. Mild coexistence is possible, but 'very easily' directly opposes marked emotional disorganization on recall and is clinically inconsistent within the same node.

issues.item: Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy 'Avoid Police' is poorly aligned with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a combat trauma in a 21-year-old nurse, avoidance of police is not supported by the listed triggers, threat items, or memory content, which center on sirens, bodily arousal, transport, flashbacks, scanning, and rage/overwhelm. This looks like a strategy targeting a threat context not otherwise represented in the formulation or symptom profile.

Avoiding police is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a combat trauma survivor who is a nurse. The other selected items center on alarm, flashbacks, sirens, somatic arousal, and generalized danger scanning, but nothing else suggests police-specific threat, authority-related trauma meaning, or a law-enforcement context. This strategy appears disconnected from the trigger, threat, and memory content.

Bus riding as a selected trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear clinical link to the other chosen items. The active formulation strongly links triggers with threat and maladaptive strategies, yet the other trigger items are sirens and heart racing, and the threat/memory items emphasize flashbacking, rage, overwhelm, and danger scanning without any transport-related cueing. As selected here, this item feels insufficiently anchored to the rest of the combat-related profile.

vignette:
Keilani describes the memory not as a story, but as a collection of searing fragments that refuse to be tamed into language. She was a combat medic, only nineteen, when the ambush happened. There is the memory of the immense, deafening heat of the blast that threw her against the side of the transport, the taste of sand and diesel in her mouth, and the high-pitched whine that replaced all other sound. Then, another sound cut through the ringing: the approaching wail of the QRF siren. It was meant to be a sound of hope, but for Keilani, it is forever fused with the frantic, useless pressure of her hands on her friend’s chest, the feeling of her own heart hammering a frantic, panicked rhythm against her ribs, and a surge of pure, white-hot rage at her own powerlessness. She knows what happened, minute by minute, but when she tries to form the words, her throat closes. The overwhelm is too great, a tidal wave of emotion that threatens to pull her under, leaving only the fury floating on the surface.

Two years later, the war has followed her home into the sterile, brightly-lit corridors of the hospital where she now works as a nurse. The environment, which should feel like a place of healing, is a minefield. The shriek of an incoming ambulance siren is the most potent trigger, capable of yanking her from the present in an instant. Last week, as a trauma patient was being wheeled into the ER, the sound sent her stumbling back against a wall, the scent of antiseptic suddenly replaced by the coppery smell of blood in the dust. For a few disorienting seconds, she was no longer Keilani, the nurse, but Doc, the medic, her body tensed and ready for an impact that never came. Her colleagues see her as jumpy and detached, unaware that she is constantly running threat assessments, scanning the faces of visitors for ill intent, noting every exit, and always positioning herself at the nurses’ station so no one can approach from behind.

This constant state of alert has bled into every corner of her life. She gave up running, which she used to love, because the sensation of her own heart pounding in her chest felt indistinguishable from the terror of that day. Any form of exercise that raises her pulse is now off-limits. Her boyfriend, Mark, tries to be patient, but he doesn’t understand why she flinches at the sound of a car backfiring or why she erupts in anger over something as small as a dropped dish. He sees her scanning crowds at the mall, her eyes darting everywhere, and feels the tension in her body when they are in any enclosed space. He stopped suggesting they go to concerts or even busy restaurants. She has also begun turning down invitations to parties or celebrations with friends. The idea of feeling happy or hopeful seems dangerous, a lowering of the guard that she is certain will invite disaster. She has come to believe that the world is a fundamentally unsafe place, and her role is to simply stand watch.

The decision to seek therapy came after an incident at home. Mark had tried to surprise her with a weekend getaway, a positive event meant to bring them closer. When he revealed the plan, Keilani felt a familiar surge of panic, followed by an explosive, irrational rage. She accused him of being reckless, of not understanding the need for caution, the need to stay put where it was safe. The fight was the worst they’d ever had, and it ended with him quietly stating that he felt like he was losing her. It was in that moment of silence, seeing the hurt in his eyes, that Keilani recognized the perimeter of her life had shrunk to the size of a prison cell. She is here now, not because the fear has lessened, but because the isolation has become more frightening than the memory itself. She cannot find the words for what happened, but she is desperate to find a way to live in a world where not every loud noise is a threat and not every beat of her own heart is an alarm.
